d.title: Three jobs a test can do, and the third is the one people forget
d.caption: **Every test is a permanent liability: it must be read, maintained and kept passing for as long as the code lives** — so it pays for itself only by doing one of three jobs. The second is the one with unusual economics: **most of design pressure's value is collected *before* the test ever runs**, which is why writing it can be worth it even if you delete it afterwards. And the third is the one prose cannot do: **an executable specification cannot go stale, because staleness makes it fail.**

d.title: The test budget is wildly uneven, and a coverage percentage flattens exactly that
d.caption: **Ask what it costs if this specific line is wrong and nobody notices for a month; that number times the chance of it being wrong is the budget for that code.** The range is the point: **money arithmetic gets exhaustive table-driven tests including rounding boundaries, and a `__repr__` gets no test, ever.** Two rows are about wiring rather than logic: **an authorisation rule needs a unit test per rule *and* an integration test per endpoint proving the check is actually wired in** — because a correct rule that is not called is the breach.

d.title: 100% line coverage on a function whose other branch was never tried
d.caption: **Line coverage answers exactly one question: was this line executed? It says nothing about whether anything was asserted, whether the assertion was meaningful, or whether the other branch was tried.** Both are demonstrated: **a test with no assertion at all reports 100%**, and **the same file reports 100% on lines and 83% with `--cov-branch`, naming the missing jump as `2->4`.** Which is the minimum honest configuration — **branch coverage is one flag, and without it the number is measuring execution rather than testing.**

d.title: Five sections in a failure report, and most people read one
d.caption: **The other four are where the cause usually is.** The node id is **the exact argument to rerun just this test — copy it, do not re-run the suite.** The fixture line shows every fixture with its repr, **so a useful `__repr__` on your fakes turns it into free diagnostics.** The `E` lines' **`+ where` clauses show how each side was computed, which is how you tell a wrong value from a wrong attribute.** And the section people skip is where the answer was: **captured output, shown only on failure.**

d.title: Teardown after `yield` is skipped entirely if setup raises
d.caption: **A fixture is `@contextmanager` with a different decorator, and it has the same rule: put the `yield` inside a `with`, so cleanup survives an exception in the test.** The failure mode is the one people do not plan for: **if the setup *before* the `yield` raises, the code after it never runs — so a half-created resource is never cleaned up**, and the next test inherits it. Which is why **acquiring two resources in one fixture is a bug waiting to happen, and `ExitStack` or two fixtures is the fix.**

nodes.label: And the next test inherits it
Put the yield inside a with

d.title: A factory fixture lets each test override only what it cares about
d.caption: **It keeps the defaults in one place and lets the test state only the field under test** — so `make_order(total=0)` says, in the call itself, that this test is about a zero total and nothing else. The alternative is **a twelve-field constructor call in every test, where a reader cannot tell which field matters.** And the structural advantage over a plain fixture: **a factory can be called more than once per test**, which is what you need for “two orders from the same customer” — a value fixture gives you one object.

nodes.label: And it can be called twice
A value fixture gives you one object

d.title: A parallel `ids` list drifts the moment someone inserts a case
d.caption: **Prefer `pytest.param` — a separate `ids` list goes out of alignment as soon as a case is inserted in the middle, and the resulting mislabelled failure sends you to the wrong row.** With `pytest.param(..., id="zero total")` the name travels with the data and cannot drift. Which matters because **the id is what a CI failure gives you**: `test_price[zero total]` is actionable from a log, **and `test_price[3]` means opening the file and counting.**

state: no - it travels with the data

d.title: Four marks, and only `xfail` keeps running the case
d.caption: **`xfail` runs the test and records the expected failure, so the case still documents the requirement and reports when it starts passing** — which `skip` cannot do, because a skipped test tells you nothing about the code. **`strict=True` is the version to prefer: an unexpected pass *fails* the suite, forcing the marker to be removed** rather than left in place for a year after the bug was fixed. And the last row is the warning: **deleting the case loses the requirement it documented, which is almost never what you want.**

d.title: monkeypatch for values, patch for callables you will assert on
d.caption: **`monkeypatch` has no mock machinery — no `assert_called_with`, no `return_value`, no call list — which is exactly why it is the right tool for a value: it sets it, and undoes it after the test.** `patch` is for a callable whose *calls* you want to inspect. And the row that matters more than either: **time and randomness should be injected rather than patched** — take `now` or `rng` as a parameter, because patching `datetime` reaches every module that imported it, including ones you did not mean to affect.

state: a Mock, with a call list

d.title: Three assertions that pass while checking nothing
d.caption: **`assert_called_with` checks only the *most recent* call, so a test passes while missing an earlier wrong one — `assert_has_calls` or `call_args_list` is what you want when there was more than one.** The three that silently do nothing are worth memorising, because they look right: **any method misspelled on a `Mock` returns another `Mock` and therefore passes** — `assert_called_once` with a typo, `assert_called` on a `MagicMock` attribute that was never configured, and the classic **`assert mock.called_once` which is an attribute access, not a call.**

d.title: Seven test symptoms, each naming a specific design fault
d.caption: **Test pain is a measurement, not an inconvenience — each symptom names something the design is doing.** The two most common: **several `@patch` decorators mean the function constructs its own dependencies**, and **patching `datetime` or `random` means it reads a hidden global source.** Both fix the same way: pass it in. And the sixth is the subtle one: **asserting on log output to verify a decision means the decision has no return value** — so return it, and log it at the caller.

d.title: A default argument is a complete dependency-injection system
d.caption: **No container, no decorator, no framework** — a parameter with a default keeps every existing call site working and gives every test a substitution point. Which is 3.2's keyword argument doing the job a Java codebase needs a framework for, and it has one real advantage over a constructor: **the substitution is visible in the signature, so a reader can see what the function depends on without reading the body.** The limit is the usual one: **once three or four dependencies travel together, a constructor or a small object reads better.**

nodes.label: Every existing call site still works
And every test has a substitution point
Past three or four: a constructor

d.title: All four have the same shape: something the function reaches out to grab
d.caption: **A module-level client, `datetime.now()`, `os.environ`, a global cache — all four are things the function reaches out to grab rather than being handed, and injecting each one is a small change that also documents the dependency.** The pattern for code that genuinely must touch the world is the humble object: **put the untestable part in a thin wrapper with no logic, and test the logic it calls.** Which is the honest limit — **you are not making I/O testable, you are making sure almost nothing depends on it.**

d.title: The container is the fixture, started once per session
d.caption: **A session-scoped container plus a per-test transaction that rolls back is the correct arrangement: the whole startup cost is paid once and every test still gets a clean database.** The detail that makes it work is `join_transaction_mode`, **which keeps the test's outer transaction in charge even when the code under test commits** — without it, application code calling `commit()` escapes the rollback and leaks state into the next test. And the SQLite substitution is the trade to make knowingly: **faster, and a different SQL dialect, so the things it cannot catch are exactly the dialect-specific ones.**

nodes.label: Without it a commit() escapes
nodes.sub: and leaks into the next test

d.title: State only what the test is about
d.caption: **The alternative is a twelve-field constructor call in every test, where a reader cannot tell which field matters** — so a factory makes the significant value the only visible one. And the warning next to it is about the opposite failure: **shared fixture data is the slow poison.** A module-level `sample_orders` that forty tests read becomes **something nobody can change, because any edit breaks an unrelated test** — and the tests that depend on its incidental properties are the ones that break. **Build per test; share only the expensive infrastructure.**

nodes.label: Against twelve fields in every test

d.title: Six techniques, and the first one has no cost at all
d.caption: **A session-scoped container with a per-test transaction costs nothing — it is simply correct**, which is why it is first. `pytest-xdist` is near-linear across cores **and needs a database or schema per worker**, which is the whole setup cost. The row worth being honest about is the last: **reusing the container across runs saves two seconds per local run and leaves a stale schema when migrations change** — a trade that is fine until the day it costs you an hour of confusion.

steps.code: a template database restored per test

d.title: `parallel = true` is the one people miss, and without it coverage collapses
d.caption: **Run under `pytest-xdist` without `parallel = true` and each worker overwrites the last coverage file, so the number reports whatever the last worker happened to run** — a plausible figure that is measuring one fragment of the suite. The pairing is `parallel = true` plus `coverage combine`. And the honest part of the configuration is what you exclude: **every `# pragma: no cover` is a line nobody will ever be told about again**, so the cost of excluding is not the percentage, it is the silence.

nodes.sub: is a line you silenced forever

d.title: `fail-fast: false` is deliberate, and the step order is a design decision
d.caption: **The matrix default cancels the other Python versions on the first failure, so you learn that 3.11 broke and not whether 3.12 did** — `fail-fast: false` costs a few minutes of CI and tells you whether the failure is version-specific, which is the question you were going to ask next. And the ordering: **lint and type-check before the tests, because they are seconds against minutes and catch a different class of error** — so a run that will fail anyway fails fast, and a developer gets the cheap feedback first.
